Abstract

System logs are a rich source of information. The complexity and amount of data contained in log files is increasing rapidly,
especially with the development of cloud computing in clustered environments. Log analysis is effective to find the root cause of an
issue. Because of the huge volume of unstructured logs, manual inspection becomes difficult and time consuming. Hence, there is a
need to automate the process of log analysis. Current state-of-the-art deep learning-based techniques are trained on generic datasets
and do not perform well on specific system logs. The proposed invention is focused to predict errors from large system specific logs
by using manual vectorization technique called “LogWord2Vec” and combining it with data-cleaning, augmentation, embedding,
and deep learning method together. Unlike other solutions, our method does not require a large dataset, and works well on medium
to small sized datasets. The proposals described in this disclosure help in improving both the accuracy and the efficiency of log
parsing systems. We have used combination of Convolution neural network (CNN) layer and long short-term memory (LSTM)
layer to build the model and obtained accuracy of 99.19% with 0.81% of misclassification. © 2023 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0)

#### _2.2. Learnable Solutions_ 

Existing solutions include training models (including CNN/RNN networks) on log datasets. These models are capable of extracting features from given text data and classify error/non-errors from logs. For this method the logs need to be normalized and converted to numerical features to be given as input to these models. Text vectorization can be accomplished using a variety of existing numerical encoding methods, that are listed below, 

**_One Hot Encoding (OHE)_** _._ It does not consider the frequency or weight of the words while representing the text as vector. Here, each unique word is represented as 1, if it is present in the text line, else 0. It produces a highdimensional and sparse vector. The dimension’s size is equal to the vocabulary’s number of words, and the majority of the elements are zero. The word-relationship between words is lost, and the syntactic and semantic commonality between words cannot be adequately represented, despite the fact that the text can be treated as a vector . That’s why this method is very rarely or not used now instead other word embedding methods are used for text vectorization, which are explained below. **_Term Frequency_** _._ Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) : Unlike One Hot Encoding, this technique considers the frequency of words and accordingly gives a score to all the unique words present in the corpus. It provides less weight to words that appear frequently throughout the corpus and more weight to terms that appear frequently in a single document rather than across the entire corpus. Sandhu, A.

been applied before LogWord2Vec. In our proposed augmentation technique we are oversampling the minority class
data sample by replacing the words int text line with their synonyms so, developers do not need to follow specific
word constraint and thus our proposed augmentation solution is not limited to developer’s vocabulary of logs and
handling both specific word as well as synonyms constraint. Using data augmentation, our solution can be applied to
any unbalanced or small dataset without any data redundancy. We are using left padding instead of right padding to increase the size of vector so that, all vectors have same length
as shown in Fig. 3. In case of left padding, as shown in Fig. 7, sequential models such as RNN and LSTM can recover
from noise that has been added by the continuous zero values seen in the beginning of the vector. This is because it
has a sequence of non-zero values towards the end of the vector to learn the pattern and recover from the added noise. 3. Methods and Materials

5. Conclusion

In this study, we proposed a constructive log classification solution pipeline using a combination of CNN and
LSTM layer. We used data augmentation technique for data balancing and “LogWord2Vec” numerical encoding for
vectorization. Our unique “LogWord2Vec” vectorization uses left padding and ensures that the previous obtained
pattern of any vector sequence is not lost unlike others that use right padding. Using our technique, 0.33% of validation
error are reduced which resulted in a better accuracy compared to TensorFlow text vectorization. The number of
misclassifications have reduced by approximately 19%. SIDEBAR: Fig.

This work was supported by the Swedish Knowledge Foundation within the research profile NIIT. ABSTRACT
The rapid progress in sensor technology and computational capabilities has significantly
improved real-time data collection, enabling precise monitoring of various phenomena and industrial
processes. However, the volume and complexity of heterogeneous data present substantial processing
challenges. Traditional data-processing techniques, such as data aggregation, filtering, and statistical
analysis, are increasingly supplemented by data fusion methods. These methods can be broadly categorised
into traditional analytics-based approaches, like the Kalman Filter and Particle Filter, and learning-based
approaches, utilising machine learning and deep learning techniques such as Artificial Neural Networks
(ANN) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). These techniques combine data from multiple sources
to provide a comprehensive and accurate representation of information, which is critical in number of
fields. Despite this, a comprehensive review of learning-based, particularly deep learning-based, data fusion
strategies is lacking. This paper presents a thorough review of deep learning-based data fusion methodologies
across various fields, examining their evolution over the past five years. It highlights applications in remote
sensing, healthcare, industrial fault diagnosis, intelligent transportation, and other domains. The paper
categories fusion strategies into early-level, intermediate-level, late-level, and hybrid fusion, emphasising
their synergies, challenges, and suitability. It outlines significant advancements, the comparative advantages
of deep learning-based methods over traditional approaches, and emerging trends and future directions. To ensure a comprehensive analysis, the review is structured using the ProKnow-C methodology, a rigorous

However, regardless of the type of multi-sensor data, several challenges—such as data imperfections, imprecision, outliers, and uncertainty—must be considered . Data fusion, which typically involves combining data from multiple sources to form a more comprehensive and accurate representation of information , , , , addresses these challenges. For instance, data from autonomous vehicles can be merged for improved object detection, tracking, and assessments. Similarly, data fusion is widely used in fields such as remote sensing, healthcare , industrial fault diagnosis, and intelligent transportation. This integration of data from various sources, ranging from optical sensors to radar, lidar, and cameras, enhances decisionmaking, detection accuracy, traffic and route management, weather predictions, diagnosis, and environmental perception and navigation. In addition to how and where data fusion occurs, there are two main approaches to data fusion integration algorithms: traditional data fusion approaches, also known as analytics-based data fusion, and learning-based data fusion. Traditional approaches include techniques such as the Kalman Filter, Particle Filter, and Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence , , , . Learning-based data fusion utilises machine learning and Deep Learning (DL) methods such as Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), fuzzy logic, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) . Meng et al. provide a comprehensive review of the literature on this topic. They introduce basic concepts and background knowledge of data fusion and machine learning, proposing a set of criteria to evaluate the performance of data fusion methods, including efficiency, quality, stability, robustness, extensibility, privacy, and testing with real-world datasets. These criteria are used to assess the strengths and weaknesses of various machine learning-based data fusion methods reviewed in their paper. Gao et al. focus on deep learning models instead, specifically architectures designed for multi-modal data fusion. A more recent comparative review by Tang et al. categorises DL-based inference mechanisms into five groups: adaptive learning, deep generative, deep discriminative, algorithm unrolling, and transformer models. While Tang et al. discuss different application domains, their focus is on the use of public datasets and the performance of deep learning algorithms rather than fusion strategies and approaches. There is a notable gap in the literature: a comprehensive review of DL-based data fusion strategies across different domains. This paper aims to fill that gap by providing an in-depth review of existing DL-based data fusion strategies in various fields and explore how learning-based data fusion approaches using DL methods have evolved over the past five years. The application fields where these methods are predominantly used will be examined, in addition, there will be an analysis of how various studies have addressed the challenges using learning-based data fusion techniques, particularly with the aid of several supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement learning, and DL techniques. Challenges such as high resource consumption, the demand for massive amounts of data, use in resource-constrained devices, sensor modalities, multi-source and multi-sensor data and asynchronous data affecting such DL-based data fusion strategies will also be explored. III. DEEP LEARNING METHODS USED FOR DATA FUSION
In the evolving field of data fusion, DL architectures have
emerged as pivotal tools, offering robust methods to integrate
and interpret diverse datasets. These architectures vary
in design and applicability, addressing specific challenges
across different domains. For instance, Fully Connected Neu-
ral Networks (FCNNs) are recognised for their ability
to identify complex patterns through dense interconnections
between layers. CNNs excel in processing spatial
information, making them ideal for image and audio analysis. While, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), including Long
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Network and Gated Recurrent
Units (GRU), are tailored for sequential data, providing
memory capabilities that capture temporal dynamics . Further specialisation is seen in Graph Neural Networks
(GNN) , which are adept at handling data structured
as graphs, thus applicable in social networks and molecular
modelling. Autoencoders, including Sparse and Stacked
architectures , offer powerful dimensionality reduction
and feature learning, essential for tasks like anomaly detec-
tion. Deep Belief Networks (DBN) , utilise a layer-
wise training approach that is beneficial for unsupervised
learning in image and speech recognition. Encoder-decoder
structures , and Transformers , provide
advanced solutions for sequence-to-sequence tasks, with the
latter particularly transforming the natural language process-
ing landscape due to their parallel processing capabilities. Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) , however,
are a class of artificial intelligence algorithms used in unsu-
pervised machine learning, introduced by Ian Goodfellow
and his colleagues in 2014 . They consist of two neural
networks, the generator and the discriminator, which are
trained simultaneously through adversarial processes. The
generator creates data that is similar to a training set, while the
discriminator evaluates the authenticity of the generated data,

c5e30f30dc14b28b61143498455c92807d2f310e.text:
discriminator evaluates the authenticity of the generated data,
determining whether it resembles real data from the dataset
or not. These DL methods not only enhance the performance
of data fusion tasks but also extend the boundaries of
what can be achieved in fields ranging from healthcare
to autonomous driving, demonstrating the vast potential
of integrating multiple data sources through sophisticated
architectures. IV. DEEP LEARNING-BASED DATA FUSION STRATEGIES
With advancements in processing hardware and other data
processing technologies, machine learning techniques have
been widely adopted by researchers to improve the overall
performance of data fusion strategies to make optimal use
of the complementary, overlapping, and cooperative features
found in diverse modalities. Machine learning methods are
successfully deployed to fuse structured and unstructured
data with different statistical characteristics . In recent
years, there has been a shift from conventional machine
learning to DL for data fusion. This shift is due to the fact that
the machine learning methods commonly used for data fusion

These hierarchical fusion levels have unique advantages and drawbacks. The choice of fusion hierarchy based on the application need could influence the model’s final outcome. For example, data level fusion or early level fusion, shown in Fig. 6, gives the minimal information loss by processing a substantial volume of information; however, it is coupled with lower fault tolerance and intricate implementation of the fusion algorithm at lower levels . Conversely, intermediate-level feature fusion shown in Fig. 8 operates on a more moderate scale of information, providing better fault tolerance and a simpler implementation of the fusion algorithm. Yet, it necessitates data pre-processing or feature extraction, resulting in a medium level of information loss . In feature-level fusion, the data features from different modalities can be combined to create a cross-modal, high-dimensional data feature. However, an appropriate feature connection method such as feature vectors, pooling processing, gated filtering and other operations must be selected based on the target application , , . In late-level decision fusion shown in Fig. 10, data from different modalities is used to train separate models. To make final decisions, the outputs of local decisions from multiple models are combined. Common aggregation methods found in the literature include average output, majority voting, and weighted voting . Decision-level fusion operates on a reduced amount of information, offering commendable fault tolerance and straightforward implementation of the fusion algorithm. Nevertheless, this approach is associated with the highest degree of information loss among the fusion levels . DL model. Independent feature extraction is performed on
each type of data using specialised DL models. Common

recognition, accelerometer and gyroscope data might be pro-

extracting features independently from each data source,
the intermediate fusion layer combines these features. This
fusion can be implemented in techniques like concatenation,
which combines feature vectors from different sources along
the channel dimension , or with attention mechanisms,
which use an attention layers to weigh the importance of
different features before combining them . Statistical
methods such as canonical correlation analysis can also
be used to combine features in a statistically meaningful
way . The fused feature representation is then passed
through additional layers of the neural network for further
processing. This often includes fully connected layers, addi-
tional convolutional layers, or recurrent layers, depending on
the application, to perform the desired prediction task such as
classification or regression. 1) SYNERGIES IN IMPLEMENTING DEEP LEARNING-BASED

A novel data fusion technique proposed by focuses on enhancing automatic intake gesture detection, a critical component of dietary intake assessments. This technique employs multi-modal data from wearable inertial sensors and indoor cameras, utilising the OREBA-DIS and OREBA-SHA datasets. The study explores different levels of data fusion through three distinct models: 

- **No Fusion Model:** Independently processes each modality to make separate decisions. - **Score-level Fusion Model:** Integrates probabilities from both modalities using score-level fusion to improve prediction accuracy. - **Decision-level Fusion Model:** Combines outcomes from each modality using decision-level fusion to produce binary decisions. The core architecture comprises parallel branches for processing: a CNN-based ResNet-50 network followed by an LSTM layer for video data, and a CNN-LSTM model for inertial data. The second stage introduces a score-level fusion module for recalculating probabilities and a rule-based decision module for the decision-level fusion approach. The comparative results demonstrated that the scorelevel fusion model outperforms the alternatives, highlighting the effectiveness of advanced data fusion techniques in accurately detecting intake gestures and thus advancing dietary intake assessment methods. ### **V. ### **VI. DISCUSSION** 

Deep learning-based data fusion techniques enhance various applications by integrating multiple data types at different stages. Early-level fusion, commonly used in remote sensing, environmental monitoring, and autonomous driving, integrates data from sources such as LIDAR, radar, and cameras to improve object detection and scene understanding. This approach utilised the full context of combined features from the outset, which is beneficial for interpreting complex scenes. However, early fusion may face challenges with highdimensional data and is often less effective when dealing with heterogeneous data sources that require distinct processing. Intermediate-level feature fusion, commonly used in industrial applications such as fault diagnosis, health monitoring, and urban traffic management, combines features after initial preprocessing. This method enhances performance without the computational burden of early fusion, balancing preprocessed feature utilisation. While intermediate fusion may not capture the full context due to prior preprocessing of raw data, it enhances model robustness and accuracy by utilising complementary information from different data types. This approach is effective in applications like predicting the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of machinery and enhancing feature analysis in pre-processed video frames. Late-level decision fusion integrates decisions from various models or modalities to enhance accuracy in fields like medical diagnostics and autonomous systems. This method enhances decision-making by merging independent model outputs, increasing overall accuracy. It is particularly useful for tasks such as needle tip tracking during ultrasound-guided procedures and lung nodule classification. However, ensuring

2bfd5d1756579da1a13adb7a1d00bede9eeb3546.text: aligned decisions can be challenging, and the fusion method might reduce the specificity of individual model predictions. Hybrid fusion integrates various modalities at different processing stages, optimising feature extraction and decisionmaking. This approach offers flexibility by combining early, intermediate, and late fusions, maximising information extraction and utilisation across different stages. Hybrid fusion is utilised in complex systems like medical imaging for tumour classification and autonomous driving for road segmentation. Despite its computational complexity, which requires advanced algorithms for synchronisation and calibration, hybrid fusion often delivers higher performance metrics. Analysis shows that intermediate fusion is the most widely used approach due to its versatility and effectiveness across applications, offering a good trade-off between computational efficiency and performance. Both early and intermediate fusion are extensively used in image and video analysis. There is a growing trend toward adaptive and hybrid fusion methods that dynamically select the optimal fusion level based on application requirements. These methods use machine learning for real-time optimal fusion strategies and advanced neural networks for dynamic architecture adjustment, improving both accuracy and efficiency in predictive analytics and decision-making. DL-based data fusion improves generalisation by exposing models to varied features and data representations, reducing overfitting. Fusion techniques greatly improve performance in complex environments where multiple data types need integration. Robust fusion models are prioritised in autonomous driving, medical diagnostics, and industrial applications to ensure safety and generalisation in various conditions. Various strategies enhance the robustness of fusion models, such as data augmentation to expand training datasets, adversarial training to improve robustness against deliberate perturbations, and

The use of pre-trained networks also plays an important role in enhancing the performance of fusion models by leveraging previously learned features, reducing the need for extensive training from scratch. They are frequently used in intermediate-level fusion to extract robust features from raw data, thereby improving model accuracy and generalisation. In late-level fusion, pre-trained networks contribute to the robustness and accuracy of final decision-making by aggregating outputs from multiple modalities. Hybrid fusion strategies extensively utilise pre-trained networks to integrate diverse data sources efficiently. ### **VII. FUTURE DIRECTIONS** 

The continuous improvement of fusion-based models through innovative DL architectures and strategies indicates promising future research and applications. One key area is the development of adaptive fusion mechanisms.

a7392388a2e9ba36d359fa9a73ec9b06d2a5ab78.text: For instance, dynamic fusion selection involves creating systems that select the optimal fusion strategy based on real-time assessments of data quality and environmental conditions, enhancing both performance and robustness. In the manufacturing industry, fusing data from various stages of production —such as raw material properties, environmental conditions, and machine parameters—can lead to better and more precise control over production processes Additionally, context-aware fusion mechanisms adjust based on contextual information, such as switching between fusion levels in autonomous driving scenarios depending on whether a vehicle is in an urban or a rural environment. Another critical area is improving error handling and correction. Developing more effective methods to detect and correct errors in the early stages of the fusion process can prevent error propagation and enhance overall system robustness. Moreover, incorporating uncertainty estimation

50ffa20044cdc90434e82aee4f3ce64d30d875d8.text: into the fusion process can more effectively manage and mitigate the impact of data inaccuracies or sensor failures. Cross-modal validation and redundancy also play a significant role in this domain. Implementing cross-modal validation, where outputs from different modalities are used to cross-verify each other, robustness can be enhanced. Designing systems with inherent redundancy in data sources and fusion processes ensures system reliability even if one or more data streams fail. Given the growing sophistication of adversarial attacks, particularly in security-critical applications like autonomous driving and medical diagnostics, it is essential to enhance the robustness of fusion models against such attacks. This requires developing more sophisticated defences and making the models more resilient to adversarial attempts. Lastly, integrating generative AI with data fusion offers promising opportunities. Generative AI has shown great potential in tasks such as data augmentation, image synthesis, and image-to-image translation. Investigating the applications, challenges, and ethical considerations of incorporating generative AI into data fusion highlights its potential to significantly advance this rapidly evolving field. ### **VIII.
